title: Large nonlinear Hall effect in strained moiré structures hosting high-pseudospin fermions
authors: Srijata Lahiri, Gourab Paul, Bilal Tanatar, Saurabh Basu
abstract: We investigate the linear and nonlinear Hall response of a moiré \emph{watermill lattice}, in which stacking and twisting generate a four-band manifold near the Fermi level with suppressed group velocities at discrete magic angles. Including an inversion symmetry breaking onsite mass breaks the interlayer symmetry, opening a gap in this manifold and driving the system into a non-trivial bulk topological phase. We map the resulting phase diagram as a function of the strength of the mass and twist angle $θ$, revealing several sectors with high Chern numbers. We then introduce strain to break the residual $C_3$ symmetry of the lattice which activates a finite Berry curvature dipole and correspondingly, a nonlinear Hall response. The dipole reverses sign sharply across topological phase boundaries, producing butterfly like features when plotted against the relevant system parameters. Its magnitude substantially exceeds that reported for symmetry-broken transition metal dichalcogenides, consistent with the elevated Wilson-loop winding and enhanced quantum geometry associated with the lattice's pseudospin-$3/2$ character. We conclude by incorporating thermal effects on the Berry curvature dipole, asserting that it is an important tool for discerning topology at low temperatures.
summary: This paper theoretically investigates the nonlinear Hall effect in strained moiré watermill lattices containing high-pseudospin fermions. By introducing strain, the authors activate a Berry curvature dipole that drives a large, tunable nonlinear response. This work demonstrates how geometric properties of the lattice can be engineered to yield enhanced topological transport signatures.
main_problem: The study investigates the linear and nonlinear Hall response, particularly focusing on how strain engineering can activate a finite Berry curvature dipole in moiré structures hosting high-pseudospin fermions.
main_result: The system exhibits a large nonlinear Hall effect whose magnitude substantially exceeds that of symmetry-broken transition metal dichalcogenides. The sign reversal of the Berry curvature dipole across topological phase boundaries creates characteristic 'butterfly like features'.
method: Theoretical analysis using continuum models (Bistritzer-MacDonald formalism) to map out phase diagrams based on mass strength and twist angle, followed by incorporating strain effects.
model_or_system: The model is a moiré watermill lattice (WM), treated as a four-band manifold hosting high-pseudospin fermions. The Hamiltonian incorporates intralayer hopping terms and interlayer coupling, which are then modified by an inversion symmetry breaking mass term ($\Delta$) and uniaxial strain ($\epsilon_p$).
key_observables: Nonlinear Hall response (NLHE), Chern numbers ($C$), Berry curvature dipole (BCD).
important_parameters: Twist angle ($	heta$), onsite mass strength ($\Delta$), and applied strain ($\epsilon_p$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes only nearest-neighbor hopping processes are dominant, and the system is analyzed in the context of a four-band model.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the WM lattice structure with its various hopping bonds. The paper analyzes phase diagrams showing Chern number evolution and BCD dependence on strain/mass.
paper_structure: The work proceeds by first establishing the low-energy physics of the moiré watermill lattice, mapping out topological phases via Chern numbers using mass terms. Subsequently, uniaxial strain is introduced to break residual symmetries, activating a finite Berry curvature dipole responsible for the nonlinear Hall response.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter topology, the concept of engineering geometric responses (like the BCD) through external fields (strain) mirrors control mechanisms used in quantum optics or AMO physics to tune system Hamiltonians and induce novel collective states.

The small black hexagon denotes the MBZ generated by the relative rotation θ between the two layers. The vectors qb, qtr, and qtl represent the three momentum transfer vectors that couple the electronic states between the two layers.
